newsitem.title: USA: Lear sees break even on Ford seat supply.
newsitem.headline: Lear sees break even on Ford seat supply.

text.p: Lear Corp's top executive said Thursday the company would likely break even on its move to supply Ford Motor Co with replacement sport/utility seats after the original supplier was hit with a strike.
The company also said it did not receive any promises of future business from Ford for agreeing to provide the stop-gap measure and simply wanted to help a customer in a time of need.
"We weren't licking our chops," Lear Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Way told reporters at a briefing at the SAE International Congress and Exposition.
"All we wanted to do was help the customer, break even on the deal and hopefully long term we'll get some consideriation. It's that simple," Way said.

Lear agreed to supply second and third row seats for the Ford Expedition in early February. Ford was forced to halt production of the popular sport/utility after United Auto Workers union members struck two plants of Johnson Controls Inc, the original seat supplier, on January 28. The strike was settled last week.

Johnson Controls was prepared to continue making seats with non-union replacements, but Ford refused to accept them. It turned to Lear, an arch rival of Johnson Controls, during the first week of February.

Lear is continuing to make seats for Expeditions that Ford made without seats. Way said he expects Lear to break even on the deal. Lear, which is already a major seat supplier to Ford, "probably won't know for years" how its decision to help the automaker will pay off.
"We just helped them out in this case. Maybe we're stupid. We'll find out down the road," Way said.

Nearly all of Lear's U.S. plants are unionized, versus Johnson Controls, which is predominantly non-union. Way said Lear and Ford share the same view that it is advantageous to have a positive relationship with the union.
"We have the same approach of partnering and working with them. We plan to make the best of it," he said. "They're here to stay."

Lear is not opposing union organization efforts at two or three of the plants that came with its Automotive Industries acquisition, said Way. He said having union workforces does not increase the company's total costs.

Although Lear sometimes pays a higher base wage than its competitors, Way said the company gets benefits from improved worker cooperation, simpler job classifications, and overall better productivity.
Way said material expenditures, which account for 70 percent of costs, are a bigger factor than wage rates.
"It's not the labor rate," he said. "It's can we be as productive as anybody else. If we can, the rate is not the issue."
